title: The derivative of eˣ
keyIdea: e ≈ 2.718 is the one base for which the gradient of y = aˣ equals its height at every point, so d/dx(eˣ) = eˣ. For any base, d/dx(aˣ) = aˣ ln a, and by the chain rule d/dx(e^(kx)) = k·e^(kx), so d/dx(c·e^(kx)) = ck·e^(kx). The power rule does not apply, because the variable is in the exponent.

kid: Draw y = 2ˣ and put a tangent on it. At every point the gradient is about 0.69 times the height. For 3ˣ it is about 1.10 times the height. So somewhere between 2 and 3 there is a base where the gradient is exactly the height.
That base is e, about 2.718. On y = eˣ the gradient at any point equals the height there. At x = 0 both are 1. At x = 2 both are about 7.39. So d/dx(eˣ) = eˣ.
Now stretch it to e^(kx). The chain rule brings the k down in front, so d/dx(e^(kx)) = k·e^(kx). A number in front just stays. So d/dx(5e^(2x)) = 10e^(2x).
This is why growth like P = 50e^(0.2t) speeds up. The rate is 0.2 × P, so the bigger P gets, the faster it grows.
adult: In A level Mathematics (and IB Analysis and Approaches) students first meet e through gradients. From first principles, d/dx(aˣ) = lim [a^(x+h) − aˣ]/h = aˣ × lim (aʰ − 1)/h, so the gradient of every exponential is a fixed multiple of its height. That multiple is ln a. The number e is defined as the base for which the limit is exactly 1.

The results to know are d/dx(eˣ) = eˣ, d/dx(e^(kx)) = k·e^(kx), d/dx(c·e^(kx)) = ck·e^(kx) and, for any base, d/dx(aˣ) = aˣ ln a, since aˣ = e^(x ln a). Modelling uses the same idea: if P = P₀e^(kt) then dP/dt = kP, so the rate of growth is proportional to the size.

The most common mistake is using the power rule, writing x·eˣ⁻¹, as if eˣ were xⁿ. Other slips are forgetting the chain-rule factor k (writing e^(4x) for the derivative of e^(4x)), dropping the constant c, losing the minus sign for e^(−x), and thinking that every exponential is its own derivative, including 2ˣ.

In the lab you slide the base until gradient ÷ height = 1 and land on e, check gradient = height at several points on eˣ, shrink h to see (eʰ − 1)/h → 1 while (2ʰ − 1)/h → ln 2, stretch e^(kx) to read gradient = k × height, and build derivatives of c·e^(kx) from tiles.

familyTip: Ask your teenager to explain why the gradient of eˣ is eˣ without saying 'because it is'. A good answer uses the tangent picture: on this curve, the slope at every point is the same number as the height.

items: On y = eˣ the gradient equals the height

lab.caption: Flagship lab: slide aˣ until gradient = height to find e, test points on eˣ, shrink h in (eʰ − 1)/h, stretch e^(kx) and build derivatives.

practice.hint: On y = eˣ, compare the gradient at a point with the height there.
practice.explain: eˣ is its own derivative. x·eˣ⁻¹ applies the power rule, which is only for xⁿ, not for a variable in the exponent.

practice.prompt: f(x) = e^({k}x). f′(x) = A·e^({k}x). What is A?
practice.hint: The chain rule brings the number multiplying x down in front.

practice.prompt: f(x) = {c}e^(3x). f′(x) = A·e^(3x). What is A?
practice.hint: Keep the {c}, and multiply by the 3 that comes down.

practice.prompt: For y = 2ˣ, how does the gradient compare with the height at any point?
choices: It is about 0.69 times the height
practice.hint: d/dx(aˣ) = aˣ ln a. What is ln 2?
practice.explain: d/dx(2ˣ) = 2ˣ ln 2 and ln 2 ≈ 0.693, so the gradient is below the height. Only base e gives a ratio of exactly 1.

practice.hint: Here k = −1. What comes down in front?
practice.explain: k = −1 comes down, so the derivative is −e^(−x). The curve falls, so its gradient must be negative.

pool.prompt: Why is e the special base for exponentials?
choices: On y = eˣ the gradient equals the height
It is the largest base used
eˣ grows faster than any other aˣ
pool.hint: Think about gradient ÷ height for y = aˣ.
pool.explain: For aˣ, gradient ÷ height = ln a, which is 1 only when a = e. 3ˣ and 10ˣ grow faster than eˣ, so size is not the reason.

pool.hint: Keep the 5 and bring down the 2.
pool.explain: 5 × 2 × e^(2x) = 10e^(2x). 5e^(2x) forgets the chain rule, and 2e^(2x) drops the constant.

pool.prompt: y = e^({k}x). Find dy/dx at x = 0.
pool.explain: dy/dx = {k}e^({k}x). At x = 0, e⁰ = 1, so the gradient is {k}.

pool.prompt: P = {p}e^(2t). Find dP/dt at the moment when P = {p}.
pool.hint: dP/dt = 2 × P, so the rate is a multiple of the size.
pool.explain: dP/dt = 2 × {p}e^(2t) = 2P. When P = {p}, the rate is {=2*p}.
(e^0.001 − 1)/0.001 ≈ 1.0005, which tends to 1. That limit is what makes d/dx(eˣ) = eˣ × 1.

pool.hint: Write 3ˣ = e^(x ln 3), then use the chain rule.
pool.explain: 3ˣ = e^(x ln 3), so by the chain rule the derivative is ln 3 · 3ˣ. Only base e is its own derivative.

pool.prompt: Why does P = 100e^(0.3t) grow faster and faster?
choices: dP/dt = 0.3P, so a bigger P gives a bigger rate
The gradient of an exponential is constant
pool.hint: Differentiate and write the answer in terms of P.
pool.explain: dP/dt = 0.3 × 100e^(0.3t) = 0.3P. The rate is proportional to the size, so growth speeds up as P grows.

pool.hint: Here k = 1/2. Keep the 4 and multiply by k.
pool.explain: 4 × 1/2 × e^(x/2) = 2e^(x/2). 8e^(x/2) divides by k, and taking 1 off the exponent is the power rule slip.
